questions.title: Anterior-compartment arm muscle originating from the coracoid process
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is located in the anterior compartment of the arm and originates from the coracoid process?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brachialis, though in the anterior compartment, arises from the anterior surface of the distal humerus, not the coracoid process.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Triceps brachii is a posterior-compartment muscle entirely, arising from the scapula (long head) and the posterior humerus (medial and lateral heads) — it has no coracoid origin and is not in the anterior compartment at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Coracobrachialis is one of the anterior compartment's three flexor muscles. It arises from the apex of the coracoid process of the scapula, sharing this origin site with the short head of biceps brachii. It inserts on the medial surface of the mid-shaft of the humerus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The long head of biceps brachii arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, not the coracoid process — it is the short head, not the long head, that shares the coracoid origin with coracobrachialis.

questions.learning_objective: State that coracobrachialis originates from the coracoid process, distinguishing it from the long head of biceps brachii's supraglenoid tubercle origin.
questions.source_citation: FOMSCU Musculoskeletal, Anatomy 03 Questions and QBank, MCQ - Arm.pdf, item 1

questions.title: Arterial supply of the posterior compartment of the arm
questions.question: The main arterial supply of the posterior compartment of the arm is provided by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachial artery itself runs down the anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm; the posterior compartment is instead supplied by its own dedicated branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial artery is a forearm vessel, a terminal branch of the brachial artery beginning at the elbow — it plays no role in supplying the arm's posterior compartment.
explanations.C: Correct. The profunda brachii artery arises from the brachial artery. It then runs posteriorly through the triangular interval alongside the radial nerve into the spiral groove of the humerus. This makes it the main arterial supply of the posterior compartment of the arm, chiefly triceps brachii.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior ulnar collateral artery is a smaller anastomotic branch contributing to the network around the elbow, not the main supply of the posterior arm compartment as a whole.

questions.learning_objective: State that the profunda brachii artery is the main arterial supply of the posterior (extensor) compartment of the arm.

questions.title: Nerve injury causing elbow flexion weakness and lateral forearm sensory loss
questions.question: A patient has weakness in elbow flexion and loss of sensation over the lateral forearm. The most likely injured nerve is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median nerve does contribute to some forearm flexor motor supply, but its own cutaneous territory is the palmar hand and lateral three-and-a-half digits, not the lateral forearm skin above the wrist.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve's motor supply is mostly to intrinsic hand muscles and two forearm flexors, and its sensory territory is the medial (not lateral) hand and forearm — neither matches this presentation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the posterior (extensor) compartment and posterior forearm/hand skin; its injury classically causes wrist drop, not elbow flexion weakness or lateral forearm sensory loss.
explanations.D: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm's flexor muscles: biceps brachii, coracobrachialis, and most of brachialis. Injury here weakens elbow flexion. The same nerve then continues, after becoming superficial, as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, so its injury also produces the lateral forearm sensory loss described in this vignette.

questions.subtopic: Arm: nerve injury and sensory loss
questions.learning_objective: Identify the musculocutaneous nerve as the single nerve whose injury explains both elbow flexion weakness and lateral forearm sensory loss.

questions.title: Muscle NOT innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve
questions.question: The musculocutaneous nerve innervates all of the following muscles EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as an exception. Biceps brachii is fully supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, so this is one of the muscles the nerve does innervate.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an exception. Coracobrachialis is fully supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, which characteristically pierces through its belly on its course down the arm — again one of the muscles the nerve does innervate.
explanations.C: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and only the large medial part of brachialis; the lateral half of brachialis instead receives a contribution from the radial nerve. Because the question asks for the exception, the lateral half of brachialis — the part the musculocutaneous nerve does not (fully) supply — is the correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an exception. The medial (larger) part of brachialis is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, so this is one of the muscles/parts the nerve does innervate, not the exception being asked for.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral half of brachialis, unlike the medial half, is not (fully) supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
questions.source_citation: FOMSCU Musculoskeletal, Anatomy 03 Questions and QBank, MCQ - Arm.pdf, item 4

questions.title: Nerve at risk in mid-shaft humeral fracture (muscle supplied)
questions.question: A mid-shaft humeral fracture may damage the nerve that supplies which of the following muscles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biceps brachii is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, which runs in the anterior compartment, away from the mid-shaft humerus's posterior spiral groove where fracture-related nerve injury occurs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coracobrachialis, also musculocutaneous-nerve-supplied, sits in the anterior compartment and is not at risk from a mid-shaft fracture's typical nerve injury.
explanations.C: Correct. The radial nerve runs in the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus in direct contact with the mid-shaft of the bone, and along this course it supplies triceps brachii. A mid-shaft humeral fracture is therefore a classic cause of radial nerve injury, producing triceps weakness together with wrist drop from loss of the more distal forearm-extensor supply.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pronator teres is supplied by the median nerve, which runs anteriorly and medially in the arm and forearm, well away from the posterior spiral groove at risk in a mid-shaft humeral fracture.

questions.learning_objective: State that a mid-shaft humeral fracture risks the radial nerve, which supplies triceps brachii along its course through the spiral groove.

questions.title: Nerve giving motor supply to triceps brachii
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor supply to the triceps brachii?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies two forearm flexors and most intrinsic hand muscles, taking no course through the posterior arm compartment where triceps lies.
explanations.B: Correct. The radial nerve is the largest branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It runs in the spiral groove of the humerus and gives motor branches to all three heads of triceps brachii along this course. It then continues distally to supply the forearm extensors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior (flexor) compartment muscles of the arm, not the posterior compartment's triceps brachii.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor around the shoulder, a different region and different muscles from triceps brachii in the posterior arm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the radial nerve is the motor supply to triceps brachii via its course through the spiral groove.

questions.title: Insertion of biceps brachii
questions.question: Which of the following is the insertion of the biceps brachii muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coracoid process is an origin site (for the short head of biceps brachii and for coracobrachialis), not biceps brachii's own insertion point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The olecranon process is the insertion of triceps brachii, a posterior-compartment muscle, not biceps brachii.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ulnar tuberosity is brachialis's insertion, not biceps brachii's — the two elbow flexors' insertion sites on the two different forearm bones are a common paired-fact confusion.
explanations.D: Correct. Biceps brachii's two heads converge into a single muscle belly that inserts via its tendon onto the radial tuberosity, with a bicipital aponeurosis fanning medially into the forearm fascia. This radial insertion is what gives biceps brachii its supinator action alongside its role as an elbow flexor.

questions.learning_objective: State that biceps brachii inserts on the radial tuberosity, distinguishing it from brachialis's ulnar tuberosity insertion.
questions.source_citation: FOMSCU Musculoskeletal, Anatomy 03 Questions and QBank, MCQ - Arm.pdf, item 7

questions.title: Insertion of brachialis
questions.question: Which of the following is the insertion of the brachialis muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coracoid process is a scapular origin site for other anterior-compartment muscles (biceps brachii short head, coracobrachialis), not brachialis's own insertion — brachialis instead originates from the distal humerus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The olecranon process is triceps brachii's insertion, a posterior-compartment muscle, not brachialis.
explanations.C: Correct. Brachialis, lying deep to biceps brachii, arises from the anterior surface of the distal humerus and inserts onto the ulnar tuberosity and the coronoid process of the ulna. Because this insertion is on the ulna rather than the rotating radius, brachialis acts as a pure elbow flexor regardless of forearm position, unlike biceps brachii's radial-insertion-dependent supinator action.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial tuberosity is biceps brachii's insertion, not brachialis's — the two elbow flexors' insertion sites on the two different forearm bones are a common paired-fact confusion.

questions.learning_objective: State that brachialis inserts on the ulnar tuberosity, explaining why it flexes the elbow regardless of forearm rotation.

questions.title: Insertion of triceps brachii
questions.question: Which of the following is the insertion of the triceps brachii muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coracoid process is an origin site for the short head of biceps brachii and coracobrachialis, not triceps brachii's insertion.
explanations.B: Correct. All three heads of triceps brachii converge into a single tendon that inserts onto the upper surface of the olecranon process of the ulna. Anconeus, a small muscle at the back of the elbow, continues triceps' action across the joint. This shared insertion is why all three heads act together as a single elbow extensor despite their separate origins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ulnar tuberosity is brachialis's insertion, a different elbow flexor, not triceps brachii's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial tuberosity is biceps brachii's insertion, not triceps brachii's.

questions.learning_objective: State that triceps brachii inserts on the olecranon process of the ulna.

questions.title: Continuation nerve of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
questions.question: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is a continuation of which nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median nerve has no lateral forearm cutaneous branch of this kind; its own cutaneous territory is the palmar hand and lateral three-and-a-half digits.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve's cutaneous territory is the medial, not lateral, side of the hand and forearm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The axillary nerve's cutaneous territory is a small patch of skin over the lower deltoid, the 'regimental badge' area, not the forearm.
explanations.D: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and most of brachialis as it descends the anterior arm. Near the elbow it becomes superficial lateral to the tendon of biceps brachii and continues onward as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. This makes the two nerves, motor musculocutaneous proximally and sensory lateral cutaneous distally, a single continuous structure.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.title: Main vein of the anterior compartment of the arm
questions.question: What is the main vein located in the anterior compartment of the arm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cephalic vein ascends on the lateral side of the arm outside the anterior compartment proper, before crossing into the deltopectoral groove.
explanations.B: Correct. The basilic vein ascends on the medial side of the forearm and arm. It pierces the deep fascia at around the middle of the arm to run within the anterior compartment alongside the brachial neurovascular bundle. At the lower border of teres major it joins the venae comitantes of the brachial artery to form the axillary vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median cubital vein is a connecting vein at the elbow, in the cubital fossa, not a vessel of the arm's anterior compartment itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The axillary vein lies proximal to the arm, in the axilla, formed by the union of the basilic vein and brachial venae comitantes at the lower border of teres major.

questions.learning_objective: State that the basilic vein is the main vein running within the anterior compartment of the arm.

questions.title: Origin of the long head of triceps brachii
questions.question: Which of the following correctly matches the origin of the long head of the triceps brachii?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The coracoid process is an origin site for the short head of biceps brachii and coracobrachialis, not the long head of triceps.
explanations.B: Correct. The long head of triceps brachii arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, just below the glenoid cavity. The lateral and medial heads instead arise from the posterior humeral shaft, above and below the spiral groove respectively. The infraglenoid origin distinguishes the long head from biceps brachii's own long head, which arises above the glenoid at the supraglenoid tubercle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The supraglenoid tubercle is the origin of the long head of biceps brachii, not triceps; this pairing, infraglenoid for triceps and supraglenoid for biceps, is a classic exam trap.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medial epicondyle of the humerus gives origin to the common flexor origin of the forearm, not to any head of triceps brachii.

questions.learning_objective: State that the long head of triceps brachii originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, distinguishing it from biceps brachii's supraglenoid origin.

questions.title: Muscle deep to biceps brachii
questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the biceps brachii in the anterior compartment of the arm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brachioradialis is a forearm muscle, distal to the arm's anterior compartment, not a muscle lying deep to biceps brachii in the arm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Triceps brachii occupies the posterior compartment of the arm, on the opposite side of the humerus from biceps brachii, not deep to it.
explanations.C: Correct. Brachialis lies directly deep to biceps brachii in the anterior compartment. It arises from the anterior surface of the distal humerus and inserts on the ulnar tuberosity of the forearm. Because its insertion is on the ulna rather than the rotating radius, brachialis acts as the elbow's true flexor regardless of forearm position, unlike biceps brachii above it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deltoid caps the shoulder, proximal to the arm, and takes no part in the anterior compartment's muscle layering.

questions.learning_objective: State that brachialis lies deep to biceps brachii in the anterior compartment of the arm.

questions.title: Movement spared by a posterior cord lesion in the axilla
questions.question: Hard | A lesion at the posterior cord of the brachial plexus in the axilla would MOST LIKELY affect all the following EXCEPT:

options.C: Abduction of the shoulder beyond 15 degrees

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception. Elbow extension is performed by triceps brachii, supplied by the radial nerve, a posterior cord branch, so this movement would indeed be affected.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception. Sensation over the posterior arm is carried by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm, a branch of the radial nerve, so this too would be affected by a posterior cord lesion.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the exception. Abduction of the shoulder beyond 15 degrees depends heavily on deltoid, supplied by the axillary nerve, another posterior cord branch, so this would also be affected.
explanations.D: Correct. The posterior cord's branches, the axillary and radial nerves, supply the extensor (posterior) side of the limb. Biceps brachii, an anterior-compartment flexor and supinator, is instead supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, a lateral cord branch, so a posterior cord lesion spares biceps and its supination action, making this the exception the question asks for.

questions.learning_objective: State that a posterior cord lesion spares supination by biceps brachii, since biceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cord), not the posterior cord.
questions.source_citation: FOMSCU Musculoskeletal, Anatomy 03 Questions and QBank, MCQ - Arm.pdf, item 14

questions.title: Lesion causing loss of elbow/wrist extension and posterior forearm sensation
questions.question: A patient presents with inability to extend the elbow and wrist joints, and loss of sensation over the posterior forearm. The lesion is MOST LIKELY in the:

options.A: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
options.C: Median nerve in the cubital fossa
options.D: Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle

explanations.A: Correct. The radial nerve, running in the spiral groove of the humerus, supplies triceps brachii for elbow extension, the forearm's extensor muscles including the wrist extensors, and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm for posterior forearm sensation. A lesion here explains all three deficits together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Injury to the musculocutaneous nerve at coracobrachialis would weaken elbow flexion and cause lateral, not posterior, forearm sensory loss, not the pattern described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Median nerve injury in the cubital fossa affects forearm pronation and most long finger flexors, producing neither elbow/wrist extension loss nor posterior forearm sensory loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ulnar nerve injury behind the medial epicondyle affects wrist flexion and the medial hand's intrinsic muscles and sensation, not elbow/wrist extension or posterior forearm sensation.

questions.learning_objective: Localise a lesion causing combined loss of elbow/wrist extension and posterior forearm sensation to the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

questions.title: Nerve accompanying the profunda brachii in the spiral groove
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the spiral groove of the humerus accompanied by the profunda brachii artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve runs in the anterior compartment of the arm, piercing coracobrachialis, and has no relationship to the spiral groove or the profunda brachii artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve runs down the medial side of the arm before piercing the medial intermuscular septum, taking no part in the spiral groove or accompanying the profunda brachii.
explanations.C: Correct. The profunda brachii artery arises from the brachial artery just below the lower border of teres major. It then runs posteriorly with the radial nerve through the triangular interval into the spiral groove of the humerus. The two structures accompany each other along this whole course before the artery divides to feed the anastomosis around the elbow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The median nerve runs in the anterior compartment of the arm, crossing the brachial artery, and has no relationship to the posterior spiral groove.

questions.learning_objective: State that the radial nerve accompanies the profunda brachii artery through the spiral groove of the humerus.

questions.title: Site of injury affecting both the ulnar nerve and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
questions.question: Injury to which part of the arm would MOST LIKELY affect both the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The midshaft of the humerus is classically associated with radial nerve injury in the spiral groove, on the posterior/lateral aspect, not the ulnar nerve or medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral epicondyle relates to the posterior interosseous nerve and the common extensor origin, not to the medially-running ulnar nerve or medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
explanations.C: Correct. The ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm both descend together along the medial side of the arm, close to the medial intermuscular septum. They stay superficial together before diverging near the elbow, where the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle. This shared course makes the medial side of the arm the single site most likely to injure both nerves together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deltoid region relates to the axillary nerve's territory, around the surgical neck of the humerus, not to the ulnar nerve or medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.learning_objective: State that injury to the medial side of the arm is the site most likely to injure both the ulnar nerve and the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm together.
questions.source_citation: FOMSCU Musculoskeletal, Anatomy 03 Questions and QBank, MCQ - Arm.pdf, item 17
